claim: ER stress suppressed the progression of a lethal germline tumor in C. elegans by activating the ER stress sensor IRE-1.
source: We discovered that ER stress suppressed the progression of the lethal germline tumor by activating the ER stress sensor IRE-1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including genetic and RNAi experiments.

claim: ER stress-induced tumor suppression was associated with the induction of germ cell transdifferentiation into ectopic somatic cells.
source: This suppression was associated with the induction of germ cell transdifferentiation into ectopic somatic cells.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations of somatic markers in the gonad.

claim: Transdifferentiation of tumorous germ cells restored their ability to execute apoptosis.
source: Strikingly, transdifferentiation of the tumorous germ cells restored their ability to execute apoptosis and enabled their subsequent removal from the gonad.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by SYTO12 and CED-1::GFP data showing apoptotic corpses in ER-stressed tumorous gonads.

claim: Most current tumor therapeutic strategies are based on apoptosis induction in tumor cells.
source: Whereas most of the current therapeutic strategies are based on apoptosis induction in the tumor cells, the effectiveness of these approaches is limited due to acquired apoptosis resistance (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2000, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on cancer therapy.

claim: The effectiveness of apoptosis-based therapeutic strategies is limited due to acquired apoptosis resistance.
source: Whereas most of the current therapeutic strategies are based on apoptosis induction in the tumor cells, the effectiveness of these approaches is limited due to acquired apoptosis resistance (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2000, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cancer biology literature.

claim: GLD-1 is a germline-specific QUAKING-like RNA binding protein that represses the translation of a variety of germline transcripts.
source: The gld-1 (GermLine Development defective) gene encodes a germline-specific QUAKING-like RNA binding protein, which represses the translation of a variety of germline transcripts (Jungkamp et al., 2011; Wright et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing GLD-1.

claim: GLD-1 regulates many aspects of germ cell biology.
source: Consequently, GLD-1 regulates many aspects of germ cell biology (Francis et al., 1995a, 1995b; Kadyk and Kimble, 1998; Jan et al., 1999; Hansen et al., 2004; Ciosk et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on GLD-1 function.

claim: Deficiency in gld-1 results in the formation of a proximal germline tumor that fills the gonad.
source: One of the striking consequence of a deficiency in gld-1 is the formation of a proximal germline tumor that fills the gonad (Francis et al., 1995a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and is a well-established phenotype.

claim: The gld-1 germline tumor results from re-entry of meiotic germ cells into the mitotic cell cycle instead of maturing into oocytes.
source: This germline tumor is the result of re-entry of meiotic germ cells into the mitotic cell cycle instead of maturing into oocytes (Francis et al., 1995a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous characterization of the gld-1 phenotype.

claim: Tumorous germ cells in the gld-1 model can proliferate in a growth factor-independent manner.
source: These include the ability of the tumorous germ cells to proliferate in a growth factor–independent manner (Francis et al., 1995a) and their regulation by genes homologous to known human oncogenes or human tumor suppressor genes (Pinkston-Gosse and Kenyon, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on the gld-1 tumor model.

claim: Tumorous germ cells in the gld-1 model are regulated by genes homologous to known human oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes.
source: These include the ability of the tumorous germ cells to proliferate in a growth factor–independent manner (Francis et al., 1995a) and their regulation by genes homologous to known human oncogenes or human tumor suppressor genes (Pinkston-Gosse and Kenyon, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Tumorous germ cells in gld-1-deficient animals acquired resistance to apoptosis.
source: Notably, these tumorous germ cells acquired resistance to apoptosis (Gumienny et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and confirmed by the current study's observations.

claim: Precocious germ cell transdifferentiation into ectopic somatic cells occurs at a low frequency in gld-1-deficient animals.
source: In addition, some precocious germ cell transdifferentiation into ectopic somatic cells has been reported to occur at a low frequency in gld-1-deficient animal (Ciosk et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Germ cell transdifferentiation in gld-1-deficient animals can be enhanced by manipulation of RNA binding proteins, P granule components, transcription factors and histone modifiers.
source: This transdifferentiation of the germ cells can be further enhanced by manipulation of RNA binding proteins, P granule components, transcription factors and histone modifiers; all of which regulate gene expression within the transdifferentiating germ cells themselves (Ciosk et al., 2006; Tursun et al., 2011; Patel et al., 2012; Updike et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Chemically or genetically-induced ER stress promotes germ cell apoptosis in normal (non-tumorous) C. elegans germlines.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, chemically or genetically-induced ER stress promote germ cell apoptosis in normal (i.e., non-tumorous) germlines (Levi-Ferber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the same authors.

claim: Germ cells in gld-1-deficient animals are resistant to physiological and DNA damage-induced apoptosis.
source: Nevertheless, the germ cells in gld-1-deficient animals were reported to be resistant to physiological and DNA damage-induced apoptosis (Gumienny et al., 1999), suggesting that they may have acquired global resistance to apoptosis promoting signals, a common phenomenon of transformed cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: No apoptotic corpses representing physiological germ cell apoptosis were detected in tumorous gonads in the absence of ER stress.
source: As previously reported (Gumienny et al., 1999), no apoptotic corpses representing physiological germ cell apoptosis were detected in the tumorous gonads in the absence of ER stress (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: SYTO12-labeled corpses were detected in tumorous gonads of gld-1 RNAi-treated animals exposed to ER stress induced by tfg-1 RNAi or tunicamycin.
source: However, we consistently detected SYTO12-labeled corpses in tumorous gonads of gld-1 RNAi-treated animals exposed to ER stress induced either by genetic means (i.e., tfg-1 RNAi) or by chemical means (i.e., tunicamycin) (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Tunicamycin is a specific inhibitor of N-glycosylation.
source: ER stress was induced either by treating the animals with tunicamycin (a specific inhibitor of N-glycosylation) or by treating the animals with tfg-1 RNAi (tfg-1 encodes a component of COPII-coated vesicles required for the export of cargo from the ER [Witte et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tunicamycin's mechanism of action.

claim: TFG-1 encodes a component of COPII-coated vesicles required for the export of cargo from the ER.
source: ER stress was induced either by treating the animals with tunicamycin (a specific inhibitor of N-glycosylation) or by treating the animals with tfg-1 RNAi (tfg-1 encodes a component of COPII-coated vesicles required for the export of cargo from the ER [Witte et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Treatment with tunicamycin or tfg-1 RNAi specifically induces ER stress.
source: Both treatments specifically induce ER stress (Levi-Ferber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the same authors.

claim: CED-1::GFP-engulfed apoptotic corpses were only detected in tumorous gonads upon induction of ER stress.
source: CED-1::GFP-engulfed apoptotic corpses were only detected in tumorous gonads upon induction of ER stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using the CED-1::GFP marker.

claim: GLD-1 protein levels were similarly reduced in animals treated with gld-1 RNAi along with control RNAi or tfg-1 RNAi.
source: These differences were not the result of restoration of gld-1 expression in the stressed animals as GLD-1 protein levels were similarly reduced in animals treated with gld-1 RNAi along with control RNAi or tfg-1 RNAi (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: In non-tumorous gonads, apoptotic germ cell corpses are usually detected at the turn of the gonad where oogenesis occurs.
source: First, in terms of location within the gonad—whereas in non-tumorous gonads apoptotic germ cell corpses were usually detected at the turn of the gonad, where oogenesis occurs, those detected in ER-stressed tumorous gonads were located in the proximal region of the gonad (Figure 1A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: Apoptotic corpses in ER-stressed tumorous gonads are located in the proximal region of the gonad.
source: First, in terms of location within the gonad—whereas in non-tumorous gonads apoptotic germ cell corpses were usually detected at the turn of the gonad, where oogenesis occurs, those detected in ER-stressed tumorous gonads were located in the proximal region of the gonad (Figure 1A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: SYTO12-labeled nuclei and CED-1::GFP-engulfed cells in tumorous gonads exposed to ER stress were significantly larger than those detected in non-tumorous animals.
source: In addition, in terms of size, both the SYTO12-labeled nuclei and the CED-1::GFP-engulfed cells in the tumorous gonads exposed to ER stress were significantly larger than those detected in non-tumorous animals (Figure 1A,C,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in the figures.

claim: CED-1::GFP engulfed cells in ER-stressed tumorous gonads displayed a variety of shapes, unlike the typically round engulfed germ cell corpses.
source: Furthermore, unlike engulfed germ cell corpses that are typically round, the CED-1::GFP engulfed cells in the ER-stressed tumorous gonads displayed a variety of shapes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in the figure.

claim: The apoptotic cell corpses in ER-stressed tumorous gonads are distinct from the germ cell corpses observed in non-tumorous gonads.
source: Altogether, the differences in size, shape and location suggest that the apoptotic cell corpses in ER-stressed tumorous gonads are distinct from the germ cell corpses observed in non-tumorous gonads.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in size, shape, and location.

claim: Blocking apoptosis by ced-3 inactivation resulted in the accumulation of cells with large and misshaped nuclei occupying nearly 40% of the ER-stressed gonad.
source: Strikingly, blocking apoptosis resulted in the accumulation of cells with large and misshaped nuclei occupying nearly 40% of the stressed gonad (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from DAPI staining shown in the figures.

claim: In the absence of ER stress, blocking apoptosis resulted in the accumulation of ectopic cells with large and misshaped nuclei occupying only 10% of the gonad in gld-1 RNAi-treated animals.
source: However, in the absence of ER stress, the abnormally large nuclei occupied only 10% of the gonad (Figure 2A,B), indicating that ER stress promotes their induction.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in the figures.

claim: ER stress promotes the induction of ectopic cells with large nuclei in gld-1-deficient animals.
source: However, in the absence of ER stress, the abnormally large nuclei occupied only 10% of the gonad (Figure 2A,B), indicating that ER stress promotes their induction.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ectopic cell accumulation with and without ER stress.

claim: Blocking apoptosis enabled the detection of ectopic cells within the gonads of nearly 90% of the gld-1 RNAi-treated animals examined, both under normal growth conditions and under ER stress.
source: Interestingly, blocking apoptosis enabled the detection of ectopic cells within the gonads of nearly 90% of the gld-1 RNAi-treated animals examined, both under normal growth conditions as well as under ER stress, albeit to different extents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Treatment of gld-1(q485); ced-3(n1286) double mutants with tfg-1 RNAi increased the accumulation of cells with large nuclei in the gonads.
source: Furthermore, treatment of gld-1(q485); ced-3(n1286) double mutants with ER-stress inducing tfg-1 RNAi also increased the accumulation of cells with large nuclei in the gonads (Figure 2C), recapitulating the phenomena observed in gld-1, tfg-1 and ced-3 RNAi-treated animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: ire-1 is not required for germ cell transdifferentiation per se, but is required for germ cell transdifferentiation in response to ER stress.
source: We conclude that ire-1 is not required for germ cell transdifferentiation per se. However, it is required for germ cell transdifferentiation in response to ER stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that basal transdifferentiation occurs in ire-1 mutants but ER stress-induced enhancement does not.

claim: The regulation of germ cell pluripotency by ER stress in gld-1-deficient animals requires the activation of the ER stress sensor IRE-1.
source: Furthermore, these findings indicate that the regulation of germ cell pluripotency by ER stress in gld-1-deficient animals requires the activation of the ER stress sensor IRE-1, and is not simply the result of interference with ER homeostasis and function.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic requirement for ire-1 in ER stress-induced transdifferentiation.

claim: Genetically-induced ER stress resulted in a 3-6 fold increase in the fluorescence of each of the three germ layer transgenic markers in tumorous gonads.
source: Genetically-induced ER stress resulted in a 3–6 fold increase in the fluorescence of each of the three germ layers transgenic markers in the tumorous gonads (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence data shown in the figure.

claim: Treatment with tunicamycin increased the fluorescence of the neuronal marker Punc-119::gfp in the tumorous gonads of gld-1; ced-3 deficient animals.
source: Similarly, treatment with tunicamycin increased the fluorescence of the neuronal marker Punc-119::gfp in the tumorous gonads of gld-1; ced-3 deficient animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: Ectopic somatic cells were not detected in the gonad of germ cell-deficient glp-1 animals upon induction of ER stress.
source: Ectopic somatic cells were not detected in the gonad of germ cell-deficient glp-1 animals, although they were detected in control germ cell (+) animals upon induction of ER stress (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The ectopic somatic cells induced by ER stress in the tumorous gonad are derived from the germ cells themselves.
source: These findings are consistent with the possibility that the ectopic somatic cells induced by ER stress in the tumorous gonad are derived from the germ cells themselves, uncovering ER stress as a potent regulator of germ cell pluripotency.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of ectopic cells in germ cell-deficient animals.

claim: ER stress acts as a potent regulator of germ cell pluripotency.
source: These findings are consistent with the possibility that the ectopic somatic cells induced by ER stress in the tumorous gonad are derived from the germ cells themselves, uncovering ER stress as a potent regulator of germ cell pluripotency.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing ER stress-induced transdifferentiation.

claim: Previously identified regulators of germ cell pluripotency act at the final steps of the transdifferentiation process by directly regulating gene expression.
source: Importantly, unlike previously identified regulators of germ cell pluripotency, all of which act at the final steps of the transdifferentiation process by directly regulating gene expression (Ciosk et al., 2006; Tursun et al., 2011; Patel et al., 2012; Updike et al., 2014); ER stress and ER homeostasis likely act further upstream, linking between cellular and organismal physiology and germ cell fate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ER stress and ER homeostasis likely act upstream of previously identified regulators, linking cellular and organismal physiology to germ cell fate.
source: Importantly, unlike previously identified regulators of germ cell pluripotency, all of which act at the final steps of the transdifferentiation process by directly regulating gene expression (Ciosk et al., 2006; Tursun et al., 2011; Patel et al., 2012; Updike et al., 2014); ER stress and ER homeostasis likely act further upstream, linking between cellular and organismal physiology and germ cell fate.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with previously identified regulators.

claim: tfg-1 RNAi failed to increase germ cell transdifferentiation in ire-1-deficient animals.
source: In contrast, tfg-1 RNAi failed to increase germ cell transdifferentiation in ire-1-deficient animals (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A low level of ectopic somatic cells was detected in gld-1; ire-1-deficient animals, similar to that observed in gld-1-deficient animals not exposed to ER stress.
source: Nevertheless, a low level of ectopic somatic cells, similar to that observed in gld-1-deficient animals that were not exposed to ER stress, was still detected in gld-1; ire-1-deficient animals (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The basal level of germ cell transdifferentiation in gld-1; ire-1-deficient animals was not increased by tfg-1 RNAi-induced ER stress or by the ER stress associated with ire-1 deficiency.
source: This basal level of germ cell transdifferentiation was not increased by tfg-1 RNAi-induced ER stress or by the ER stress associated with the ire-1 deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in ire-1 mutants.

claim: Significantly increased levels of ectopic nuclei were detected in the gonads of both xbp-1(zc12) and xbp-1(tm2457) mutants upon treatment with gld-1 and ced-3 RNAi on day 4 of adulthood.
source: Strikingly, we detected significantly increased levels of ectopic nuclei in the gonads of both xbp-1 mutants upon treatment with a mixture of gld-1 and ced-3 RNAi on day 4 of adulthood (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Deficiency in XBP1 leads to activation of the ER stress sensor IRE1 in mice and C. elegans xbp-1(zc12) mutants.
source: Previous studies in mice and in C. elegans xbp-1(zc12) mutants have demonstrated that the mere deficiency in XBP1 leads to activation of the ER stress sensor IRE1 (Hu et al., 2009; Richardson et al., 2011; Hur et al., 2012; Safra et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The high level of germ cell transdifferentiation in xbp-1 mutants was completely dependent on ire-1.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the high level of germ cell transdifferentiation in xbp-1 mutants was completely dependent on ire-1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no transdifferentiation in xbp-1; ire-1 double mutants.

claim: ER stress-induced germ cell transdifferentiation is completely dependent on ire-1 but not dependent on xbp-1.
source: Thus, although ER stress-induced germ cell transdifferentiation is completely dependent on the ER stress sensor gene ire-1, it is not dependent on its downstream target xbp-1, implying that it is mediated by an ire-1-dependent xbp-1-independent signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: ER stress-induced germ cell transdifferentiation is mediated by an ire-1-dependent xbp-1-independent signal.
source: Thus, although ER stress-induced germ cell transdifferentiation is completely dependent on the ER stress sensor gene ire-1, it is not dependent on its downstream target xbp-1, implying that it is mediated by an ire-1-dependent xbp-1-independent signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data showing ire-1 requirement but not xbp-1 requirement.

claim: xbp-1 inactivation suppressed the germline tumor in gld-1-deficient animals.
source: We found that xbp-1 inactivation, not only induced germ cell transdifferentiation but also suppressed the germline tumor; demonstrating that the two phenomena are tightly correlated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of tumor phenotypes in xbp-1 mutants.

claim: Germ cell transdifferentiation and tumor suppression are tightly correlated.
source: We found that xbp-1 inactivation, not only induced germ cell transdifferentiation but also suppressed the germline tumor; demonstrating that the two phenomena are tightly correlated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both phenomena occur together.

claim: The density of germ cells in the germline tumor was reduced in tumorous animals exposed to ER stress such that the germline tumor did not fill the entire gonad.
source: The physiological improvement was manifested in several ways: (a) the density of the germ cells in the germline tumor was reduced in the tumorous animals exposed to ER stress such that the germline tumor that occupied the proximal gonad did not fill the entire gonad (Figure 5A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in the figures.

claim: ER stress significantly delayed the paralysis of tumorous animals and allowed them to move freely at time-points where most non-stressed tumorous animals were paralyzed.
source: We find that ER stress significantly delayed the paralysis of the tumorous animals and allowed the animals to move freely at time-points where most of the non-stressed tumorous animals were paralyzed (Figure 5B, Videos 1, 2 and Figure 5—Figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by paralysis assay data shown in the figures and videos.

claim: Treatment with gld-1 RNAi shortened the lifespan of wild-type animals by more than 30%, whereas it shortened the lifespan of ER stressed-xbp-1 mutants by only 13%.
source: We found that in wild-type animals, treatment with gld-1 RNAi shortened the lifespan by more than 30%, whereas it shortened the lifespan of ER stressed-xbp-1 mutants by only 13% (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: Treatment with gld-1 RNAi shortened wild-type animals lifespan by more than 30%, whereas it shortened the lifespan of tfg-1 RNAi-treated animals by only 15%.
source: Similarly, treatment with gld-1 RNAi shortened wild-type animals lifespan by more than 30%, whereas it shortened the lifespan of tfg-1 RNAi-treated animals by only 15% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: No physiological improvement in terms of lifespan, movement or germline density were observed in ire-1 deficient animals upon xbp-1 inactivation.
source: Importantly, no physiological improvement in terms of lifespan, movement or germline density were observed in ire-1 deficient animals, in which ER stress-induced germ cell transdifferentiation does not occur, even upon xbp-1 inactivation (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The genetic requirements for suppression of the germline tumor and for induction of germ cell transdifferentiation converge on ire-1.
source: Thus, the genetic requirements for suppression of the germline tumor and for induction of germ cell transdifferentiation converge on ire-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both processes require ire-1.

claim: DNA damage, pathogens, oxidative, osmotic, heat shock, starvation and ER stress are all known inducers of germ cell apoptosis in normal (non-tumorous) germlines.
source: DNA damage, pathogens, oxidative, osmotic, heat shock, starvation and ER stress are all known inducers of germ cell apoptosis in normal (i.e., non-tumorous) germlines (Gartner et al., 2000; Salinas et al., 2006; Levi-Ferber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only treatment with tfg-1 RNAi led to the detection of cells with large nuclei in the gonads of gld-1; ced-3-deficient animals, although some treatments induced more germ cell apoptosis than tfg-1 RNAi.
source: We found that although some treatments induced more germ cell apoptosis than tfg-1 RNAi, only treatment with tfg-1 RNAi led to the detection of cells with large nuclei in the gonads of gld-1; ced-3-deficient animals (Figure 6B and black bar graphs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different stress treatments shown in the figure.

claim: The transdifferentiation of germ cells is not simply a side-effect or default fate of apoptosis-resistant tumorous cells under proapoptotic stress.
source: This indicates that the transdifferentiation of the germ cells is not simply a side-effect or a default fate of apoptosis-resistant tumorous cells under proapoptotic stress which they fail to execute.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of ER stress in inducing transdifferentiation compared to other stresses.

claim: Only treatment with tfg-1 RNAi suppressed the progression of the germline tumor among the tested stresses.
source: Moreover, since only treatment with tfg-1 RNAi suppressed the progression of the germline tumor (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), this lends further support to the notion that induction of germ cell transdifferentiation is a prerequisite for the suppression of the germline tumor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Induction of germ cell transdifferentiation is a prerequisite for the suppression of the germline tumor.
source: Moreover, since only treatment with tfg-1 RNAi suppressed the progression of the germline tumor (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), this lends further support to the notion that induction of germ cell transdifferentiation is a prerequisite for the suppression of the germline tumor.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between transdifferentiation and tumor suppression.

claim: ER stress is beneficial for the healthspan of gld-1-deficient animals as it suppresses their lethal germline tumors.
source: We find that while severe stress limits organismal survival and well-being under most circumstances, ER stress is beneficial for the animals' healthspan in gld-1-deficient animals, as it suppresses their lethal germline tumors.
evidence: This is supported by the lifespan, paralysis, and tumor density data.

claim: Knockout of hsf1 in mice has deleterious impact on organismal survival under normal growth conditions and under stress, but benefits the organism in the case of cancer.
source: This is in accordance with previous findings that a stress-inducing interference such as knockout of hsf1 in mice, which has deleterious impact on organismal survival under normal growth conditions as well as under stress, actually benefits the same organism in the case of cancer (Dai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The suppression of the germline tumor is the combined effect of germ cell transdifferentiation coupled with a limited half-life of the transdifferentiated germ cells.
source: Our findings indicate that the suppression of the germline tumor is the combined effect of germ cell transdifferentiation coupled with a limited half-life of the transdifferentiated germ cells (see model in Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and presented as a model.

claim: The limited half-life of transdifferentiated germ cells is achieved by restoring their responsiveness to apoptosis once they transdifferentiate into ectopic somatic cells.
source: The latter is achieved by restoring the responsiveness of the tumorous cells to apoptosis once they transdifferentiate into ectopic somatic cells and the subsequent removal of their ectopic somatic corpses from the gonad.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transdifferentiated cells undergo apoptosis.

claim: Although germ cell transdifferentiation normally occurs in gld-1-deficient animals, its extent is not sufficient to effectively suppress the tumor by itself.
source: Importantly, although germ cell transdifferentiation normally occurs in gld-1-deficient animals (Ciosk et al., 2006), its extent is not sufficient to effectively suppress the tumor by itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of basal and ER stress-induced transdifferentiation levels and their effects on tumor progression.

claim: Effective tumor suppression is only achieved under conditions that further enhance germ cell transdifferentiation beyond its basal level, as in the case of ER stress.
source: Effective suppression is only achieved under conditions that further enhance germ cell transdifferentiation beyond its basal level, as in the case of ER stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations comparing basal and enhanced transdifferentiation.

claim: Tumor cell transdifferentiation may serve as a protective anti-tumor mechanism.
source: All in all, our results indicate that tumor cell transdifferentiation may serve as a protective anti-tumor mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing tumor suppression through transdifferentiation.

claim: Transdifferentiation-promoting genes may effectively suppress tumors.
source: This implies that transdifferentiation-promoting genes may effectively suppress tumors.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings that transdifferentiation suppresses tumors.

claim: A major consequence of ER stress is interference with ER functions, which may directly impinge upon the production of signaling molecules such as secreted peptides, hormones, cholesterol and lipids.
source: A major consequence of ER stress is interference with ER functions, which may directly impinge upon the production of a variety of signaling molecules such as secreted peptides, hormones, cholesterol and lipids which are metabolized in the ER.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ER function.

claim: It is unlikely that interference with ER functions directly accounts for ER stress-induced germline transdifferentiation and apoptosis because these do not occur in animals under severe ER stress in the absence of ire-1.
source: However, it is unlikely that this directly accounts for ER stress-induced germline transdifferentiation and apoptosis of the germ cells as these do not occur in animals under severe ER stress in the absence of ire-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic requirement for ire-1.

claim: It is the activation of the ER stress sensor IRE-1, rather than a non-specific consequence of ER stress per se, that regulates germ cell pro-differentiation and tumor progression in gld-1-deficient animals.
source: This suggests that it is the activation of the ER stress sensor IRE-1, rather than a non-specific consequence of ER stress per se, that regulate germ cell pro-differentiation and tumor progression in gld-1-deficient animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic requirement for ire-1 and independence from xbp-1.

claim: Germ-cell transdifferentiation is mediated by an ire-1-dependent xbp-1 independent signal.
source: Furthermore, since germ-cell transdifferentiation is promoted in animal deficient in xbp-1, this indicates that it is mediated by an ire-1-dependent xbp-1 independent signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: In humans, mutations that compromise the activity or expression of RNase L have been implicated with increased susceptibility to prostate cancer.
source: Interestingly, in humans, mutations that compromise the activity or the expression of RNase L, an IRE1-related endoribonuclease, have been implicated with increased susceptibility to prostate cancer (Carpten et al., 2002; Casey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RNase L is an IRE1-related endoribonuclease that has lost specificity to xbp-1 mRNA but shares with IRE-1 its promiscuous RNase activity.
source: Unlike IRE1, RNase L has lost specificity to xbp-1 mRNA. Nevertheless, it shares with IRE-1 its promiscuous RNase activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of RNase L and IRE-1 biochemistry.

claim: Tumor-suppressive properties of IRE-1-related endoribonucleases may be evolutionarily conserved.
source: This implies that tumor-suppressive properties of IRE-1-related endoribonucleases may be evolutionarily conserved, and may not be specifically associated with one specific type of prostate cancer.
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarity between IRE-1 and RNase L and their tumor-suppressive properties.

claim: One hallmark of aggressive tumors is their adaptation to their natural primary niche.
source: One hallmark of aggressive tumors is their adaptation to their natural primary niche (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2000, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cancer biology literature.

claim: Transformation into an ectopic kind of cell may have added value in suppressing aggressive tumors compared to differentiation into a cell type normally found in the same primary niche.
source: Thus, transformation into an ectopic kind of cell, rather than differentiation into a type of cell which can normally be found in the same primary niche, may have an added value in suppressing aggressive tumors.
evidence: This is speculated based on the concept of niche adaptation.

claim: In 95% of human ovarian germline tumors, totipotent germ cells precociously differentiate into a variety of ectopic somatic cells generating teratoma.
source: Strikingly, in 95% of human ovarian germline tumors, the totipotent germ cells precociously differentiate into a variety of ectopic somatic cells generating teratoma (Koonings et al., 1989; Ulbright, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Naturally occurring teratomas are usually benign whereas the remaining 5% of human ovarian germline tumors are usually malignant.
source: These naturally occurring teratoma are usually benign whereas the remaining 5% are usually malignant (Ulbright, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: Teratoma may be a preferential germline tumor in terms of survival and fitness of the organism.
source: This suggests that teratoma may be a preferential germline tumor in terms of survival and fitness of the organism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most ovarian germline tumors are benign teratomas.

claim: Some ovarian teratomas undergo malignant transformation, but this occurs only in 1.5% of teratomas.
source: Accordingly, some of the ovarian teratoma undergo a malignant transformation which occurs after the development of the teratoma. Nevertheless, this occurs only in 1.5% of teratoma (Comerci et al., 1994; Ayhan et al., 2000; Ulbright, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The conclusions from the C. elegans tumor model are naturally applied to human germline tumor biology.
source: This suggests that the conclusions derived from our studies in the C. elegans tumor model system are already naturally applied for human germline tumor biology, as if they were selected to do so by evolution.
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarity between the C. elegans findings and human teratoma biology.

claim: The potential to suppress tumors by forcing their transdifferentiation requires the tumor cells to have differentiation potential.
source: The potential to suppress tumors by forcing their transdifferentiation requires the tumor cells to have differentiation potential.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the concept of transdifferentiation-mediated tumor suppression.

claim: In mammals, subpopulations of stem cells that maintain differentiation potential exist in many organs and tissues, albeit at low numbers.
source: In mammals, in addition to the totipotent germ cells, subpopulations of stem cells, which maintain differentiation potential (i.e., pluri or multi-potent) exist in many organs and tissues, albeit at low numbers (Reya et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to stem cell biology literature.

claim: Within tumors and hematological cancers, one can find a subpopulation of cancer stem cells that possess stem cell characteristics, including the ability to give rise to a variety of cell types.
source: Furthermore, within tumors and hematological cancers, one can find a subpopulation of cancer stem cells that possess stem cells characteristics, including the ability to give rise to a variety of cell types (Reya et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to cancer stem cell literature.

claim: Differentiation therapy has been used in the clinic and is proven to be effective in limiting some kinds of tumors.
source: Accordingly, differentiation therapy has been used in the clinic and is proven to be effective in limiting some kinds of tumors (Sell, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: Current differentiation therapies induce differentiation of cells within the same lineage.
source: Interestingly, whereas these treatments induce differentiation of cells within the same lineage, induction of transdifferentiation into a completely different cellular lineage may be even more effective by creating a discrepancy and maladaptiveness between the tumorous cells and their surrounding niche.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the proposed transdifferentiation approach.

claim: Induction of transdifferentiation into a completely different cellular lineage may be more effective than same-lineage differentiation by creating discrepancy between tumorous cells and their surrounding niche.
source: Interestingly, whereas these treatments induce differentiation of cells within the same lineage, induction of transdifferentiation into a completely different cellular lineage may be even more effective by creating a discrepancy and maladaptiveness between the tumorous cells and their surrounding niche.
evidence: This is speculated based on the concept of niche adaptation.

claim: Induction of tumor cell transdifferentiation has the potential to be applied as a novel approach to combat cancer and overcome the escape of tumor cells from the cell death machinery in a wide variety of tissues.
source: Thus, induction of tumor cell transdifferentiation has the potential to be applied as a novel approach to combat cancer and overcome the escape of tumor cells from the cell death machinery in a wide variety of tissues.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental findings and their potential therapeutic implications.

claim: Under ER stress conditions, cells that expressed the neuronal marker co-localized with cells in the gonad that had atypically large nuclei.
source: We found that under ER stress conditions, the cells that expressed the neuronal marker co-localized with the cells in the gonad that had atypically large nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by co-localization experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No expression of the Punc-119::gfp somatic marker was detected in regions of the gonad devoid of large-nucleated cells.
source: No expression of the Punc-119::gfp somatic marker was detected in regions of the gonad devoid of large-nucleated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Some of the engulfed cells in the stressed tumorous gonad also expressed the somatic marker.
source: Indeed, some of the engulfed cells also expressed the somatic marker (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by co-expression experiments shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The ectopic somatic cells that arise in the stressed tumorous gonad normally undergo apoptosis and are consequently engulfed and cleared from the gonad.
source: These findings are consistent with the interpretation that the ectopic somatic cells that arise in the stressed tumorous gonad normally undergo apoptosis and are consequently engulfed and cleared from the gonad.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of engulfed cells expressing somatic markers.

claim: The teratoma contains somatic cells of different germ-layers, so only a fraction can be detected using somatic markers of specific tissues or germ layers.
source: Why was the expression of the intestinal somatic marker apparent only in some of the ced-1::gfp labeled phagosomes and not in all of them? Likewise, why weren't all the large-nucleated cells co-localized with the cells in the gonad that expressed the neuronal marker? These phenomena are likely the consequence of the fact that the teratoma contains somatic cells of the different germ-layers, implying that only a fraction of the teratoma cells can be detected using somatic markers of specific tissues or germ layers.
evidence: This is inferred to explain why not all ectopic cells express a given somatic marker.
